Suppose we fit a straight line to the M-\(\sigma\) relation. The fit gives a slope and an intercept, but a theorist who compares the slope with a prediction needs more than these two numbers. An observer who predicts the black hole mass of a new galaxy needs more too. Both need to know how well the data constrain the line. Two data sets can give similar best-fit lines and still constrain them very differently, as Figure 5.1 shows.

Frequentist methods can supply this uncertainty, for example with the bootstrap of Chapter 3. They can work well for large, well-sampled data sets. The bootstrap is harder to use in astronomy. Samples are often small or expensive to obtain, and different measurements can have very different uncertainties. The bootstrap also has no direct way to include prior knowledge.

The Bayesian approach takes a different view. It treats the model parameters as random variables with probability distributions, instead of fixed quantities whose sampling distribution we must estimate. This probabilistic view has three advantages for astronomy.

First, it gives the uncertainties of the parameters and of the predictions directly, and it needs no resampling. Second, it lets us include prior knowledge from earlier observations, theoretical constraints or physical intuition. Third, an informative prior acts as a regularizer. It penalizes very complex models unless the data require them, so it protects against overfitting without any ad hoc constraint.

We build the method in steps. Conjugate priors give posteriors in closed form for simple problems, and they show how Bayesian updating works. We then extend conjugacy to the multivariate Gaussians that linear regression needs. Next we derive the posterior of the regression weights and show that the prior acts as a regularizer. Finally we predict with full uncertainties through the posterior predictive distribution.

5.1 From Maximum Likelihood to Bayesian Inference

Bayes’ theorem gives the complete probability distribution of the model parameters. In symbols, with \(\mathbf{w}\) the parameters and \(\mathcal{D}\) the data, it reads \[ p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D}) = \frac{p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})p(\mathbf{w})}{p(\mathcal{D})}. \]This short equation tells us how to learn from data. Each part has a clear interpretation.

The likelihood \(p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})\) is the function we used in maximum likelihood estimation. It describes what the data tell us about the parameters. The prior \(p(\mathbf{w})\) expresses our beliefs about the parameters before we see the data, such as earlier results or physical constraints. The evidence \(p(\mathcal{D})\) is the integral of the likelihood times the prior over all parameter values, and it normalizes the posterior. The evidence is also called the marginal likelihood. The posterior \(p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D})\) is our updated belief after we combine the prior knowledge with the data.

Bayes’ theorem balances different sources of information. With strong prior knowledge and weak data, the posterior stays close to the prior. With a weak prior and strong data, the likelihood dominates the posterior. The posterior also shows our confidence. A narrow posterior means well-constrained parameters, and a broad posterior signals high uncertainty.

For the M-\(\sigma\) relation, the posterior might give a slope of \(4.0 \pm 0.3\) instead of the single value 4.0. For a Gaussian posterior, \(4.0 \pm 0.3\) is a 68% credible interval, the range that holds 68% of the posterior probability. Unlike a confidence interval (Section 2.6), it gives our degree of belief in the parameter itself. With such an interval we can plan follow-up observations and propagate the uncertainty through later calculations.

5.2 Conjugate Priors

Bayes’ theorem says what to compute. It does not say how. The evidence is an integral over all parameter values, and the posterior mean and variance need integrals too. These integrals can be intractable for many combinations of priors and likelihoods.

Conjugate priors solve this problem for many useful cases. A prior is conjugate to a likelihood when the posterior belongs to the same family as the prior. Only the parameters change. For example, a Gamma prior and a Poisson likelihood give a Gamma posterior. Conjugacy allows analytical solutions to inference problems that would otherwise be hard.

The evidence does not depend on \(\mathbf{w}\), so Bayes’ theorem in proportional form reads \[ p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})p(\mathbf{w}). \]

With a conjugate prior, the abstract idea of “updating beliefs” becomes a concrete update of parameters that we can compute analytically.

We build intuition with two examples that often arise in astronomical data analysis.

Poisson-Gamma Conjugacy

Suppose we count stars in different regions of the sky to measure the stellar density. Let \(\lambda\) be the expected number of stars in a region, which is the average count we would find over many similar regions.

When we observe one region, the probability of counting exactly \(n\) stars follows a Poisson distribution \[ p(n|\lambda) = \frac{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda}}{n!}. \]This distribution arises when we count rare, independent events, as we do for star counts in a field of view. The parameter \(\lambda\) depends on the stellar density of the region and on the selection effects that set how many stars we detect.

We do not know the true value of \(\lambda\). We want to learn it from the observations. Before we observe, we may hold prior beliefs about \(\lambda\) from earlier surveys, theoretical models of star formation, or the known properties of the region.

We can express these prior beliefs with a Gamma distribution of shape \(\alpha\) and rate \(\beta\) \[ p(\lambda) = \frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\lambda^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta\lambda}. \]The parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) connect directly to our prior knowledge. The ratio \(\alpha/\beta\) is our prior expectation for the star count, and the prior variance is \(\alpha/\beta^2\). The individual values of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) set our confidence in this expectation. We can think of \(\alpha\) as the total number of stars “effectively observed” in earlier surveys, and of \(\beta\) as the number of regions surveyed. If earlier surveys of 2 regions suggest about 5 stars per region, we might use \(\alpha = 10\) and \(\beta = 2\).

Conjugacy pays off when we update our beliefs with a new observation. Suppose we count \(n\) stars in a new region. Bayes’ theorem gives \[ p(\lambda|n) \propto p(n|\lambda)p(\lambda) \propto \lambda^n e^{-\lambda} \cdot \lambda^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta\lambda}. \]

Combining the terms gives \[ p(\lambda|n) \propto \lambda^{(n+\alpha-1)}e^{-(\beta+1)\lambda}. \]This is another Gamma distribution. The posterior is \(\text{Gamma}(\alpha + n, \beta + 1)\), so the parameters update by two simple rules. The parameter \(\alpha\) increases by the number of stars observed, \(n\). The parameter \(\beta\) increases by 1, because we have surveyed one more region.

Our prior \(\text{Gamma}(10,2)\) suggests about 5 stars per region from earlier surveys of 2 regions. If we observe 8 stars in a new region, the posterior is \(\text{Gamma}(18,3)\). This suggests a slightly higher average of about 6 stars per region (\(18/3 = 6\)). The estimate uses both the prior knowledge and the new evidence. Figure 5.2(a) shows this update.

Panel (b) repeats the update for a broader and a narrower prior, both with a mean of 5 stars per region. The broad prior, \(\text{Gamma}(5,1)\), stands for one earlier region, and the narrow prior, \(\text{Gamma}(20,4)\), stands for four. More earlier surveys mean a stronger belief. The narrow prior therefore holds the posterior mean at 5.6, close to the prior mean. The broad prior lets the new count pull it up to 6.5.

The update extends directly to multiple observations. If we count \(\{n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_N\}\) stars in \(N\) independent regions, the posterior is \(\text{Gamma}(\alpha + \sum_{i=1}^N n_i, \beta + N)\). This matches our intuition, because the estimate uses the total star count and the number of regions.

Bernoulli-Beta Conjugacy

Consider a second task in astronomy, the classification of galaxies as spiral or elliptical. This binary classification shows conjugacy in a different setting.

For a single galaxy, the classification has two outcomes, spiral or elliptical. Such an event follows a Bernoulli distribution, in which each outcome has a fixed probability. Let \(\theta\) be the probability that a randomly selected galaxy in our survey region is spiral. Then \[ p(x|\theta) = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}, \] where \(x = 1\) for a spiral galaxy, which has probability \(\theta\), and \(x = 0\) for an elliptical galaxy, which has probability \(1-\theta\).

We can express our prior beliefs about \(\theta\) with a Beta distribution \[ p(\theta) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}. \]Like the Gamma parameters, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) have a simple meaning. They act like counts of earlier classifications. If we had classified \(\alpha + \beta\) galaxies before, with \(\alpha\) spiral and \(\beta\) elliptical, the Beta prior would encode this history.

Now we observe \(N\) new galaxies, with \(\sum x_i\) spiral and \(N - \sum x_i\) elliptical. The likelihood is \[ p(\{x_i\}|\theta) = \theta^{\sum x_i}(1-\theta)^{N-\sum x_i}. \]

The posterior is then \[ p(\theta|\{x_i\}) \propto \theta^{\sum x_i}(1-\theta)^{N-\sum x_i} \cdot \theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1} = \theta^{(\alpha+\sum x_i)-1}(1-\theta)^{(\beta+N-\sum x_i)-1}. \]Once again we obtain a distribution from the same family, \(\text{Beta}(\alpha + \sum x_i, \beta + N - \sum x_i)\). The update rules are equally simple. The parameter \(\alpha\) increases by the number of spiral galaxies observed. The parameter \(\beta\) increases by the number of elliptical galaxies.

These examples show the pattern that makes conjugate priors useful. We can update our beliefs analytically, and each parameter update has a clear meaning as accumulated evidence. This simplicity matters when we extend the idea to linear regression.

5.3 Gaussian-Gaussian Conjugacy in One Dimension

Poisson-Gamma and Bernoulli-Beta conjugacy handle discrete data. Linear regression has continuous data with Gaussian noise, so we need Gaussian-Gaussian conjugacy.

We start with the simplest case, estimating the mean of a Gaussian distribution when the variance is known. This may seem artificial, but it contains the elements we need for linear regression. Its simplicity lets us focus on the mathematics.

Consider one observation \(x\) from a Gaussian with unknown mean \(\mu\) and known variance \(\sigma^2\) \[ p(x|\mu) = \mathcal{N}(x|\mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]This likelihood tells us how probable the value \(x\) is for any proposed mean \(\mu\). The quadratic term in the exponent makes the likelihood fall quickly as \(\mu\) moves away from \(x\). The measurement variance \(\sigma^2\) sets the rate of this decrease.

To complete the Bayesian model, we need a prior for \(\mu\). A common choice is another Gaussian distribution \[ p(\mu) = \mathcal{N}(\mu|\mu_0, \tau_0^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\tau_0^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau_0^2}\right), \] where \(\mu_0\) is our prior belief about the mean and \(\tau_0^2\) is our prior uncertainty.

Why choose a Gaussian prior? It is mathematically convenient, and it is also a sensible default when we are uncertain about a continuous parameter. A Gaussian gives the highest probability to values near our best guess \(\mu_0\) and lower probability further away. The variance \(\tau_0^2\) controls how confident we are in the prior.

Now we combine the prior and the likelihood. Both are Gaussian, so their product is also Gaussian. This is the property that conjugacy needs. We show it by multiplying the distributions and dropping normalization constants \[\begin{aligned} p(\mu|x) &\propto p(x|\mu)p(\mu) \\ &\propto \exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \exp\left(-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau_0^2}\right) \\ &\propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2} + \frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{\tau_0^2}\right]\right). \end{aligned}\]

To show that the product is Gaussian in \(\mu\), we expand the exponent and collect powers of \(\mu\) \[\begin{aligned} -\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2} + \frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{\tau_0^2}\right] &= -\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\mu^2-2x\mu+x^2}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu^2-2\mu_0\mu+\mu_0^2}{\tau_0^2}\right] \\ &= -\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}+\frac{1}{\tau_0^2}\right)\mu^2 - 2\left(\frac{x}{\sigma^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2}\right)\mu + \text{const}\right]. \end{aligned}\]This quadratic form in \(\mu\) confirms that the posterior is Gaussian. To find its parameters, we compare it with the standard form \(\mathcal{N}(\mu|\mu_1,\tau_1^2)\), which has the exponent \[ -\frac{1}{2\tau_1^2}(\mu-\mu_1)^2 = -\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{\tau_1^2}\mu^2 - \frac{2\mu_1}{\tau_1^2}\mu + \frac{\mu_1^2}{\tau_1^2}\right]. \]Comparing coefficients gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{\tau_1^2} &= \frac{1}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau_0^2}, \\ \frac{\mu_1}{\tau_1^2} &= \frac{x}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2}. \end{aligned}\]

Solving for the posterior parameters gives \[\begin{aligned} \tau_1^2 &= \left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau_0^2}\right)^{-1}, \\ \mu_1 &= \tau_1^2\left(\frac{x}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2}\right). \end{aligned}\]These update equations show the structure of Gaussian conjugacy. The posterior precision (inverse variance) \(1/\tau_1^2\) is the sum of the likelihood precision \(1/\sigma^2\) and the prior precision \(1/\tau_0^2\). Our total confidence comes from combining our prior knowledge with what we learn from the data.

The posterior mean \(\mu_1\) is a weighted average of the observation \(x\) and the prior mean \(\mu_0\). The weights are proportional to their precisions. More precise information has more influence on the final estimate, as we would expect. Figure 5.3 shows the update for two priors. To build intuition, we consider two extreme cases.

Uninformative Prior (\(\tau_0^2 \to \infty\))

When we are very uncertain about our prior belief, the posterior becomes \[\begin{aligned} \tau_1^2 &\to \sigma^2, \\ \mu_1 &\to x. \end{aligned}\] The data dominate the posterior. Our final estimate equals the observation, and its uncertainty equals the measurement error.

Very Uncertain Measurement (\(\sigma^2 \to \infty\))

When our measurement is very noisy, the posterior becomes \[\begin{aligned} \tau_1^2 &\to \tau_0^2, \\ \mu_1 &\to \mu_0. \end{aligned}\] We learn almost nothing from such a measurement, so the posterior stays close to our prior beliefs.

Multiple Observations

For multiple observations \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N\), we assume that each is drawn independently from \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). The likelihood is then a product of single-observation likelihoods. We write \(\bar{x} = (1/N)\sum_{i=1}^N x_i\) for the sample mean. The sum of squares splits as \[ \sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \mu)^2 = N(\mu - \bar{x})^2 + \sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \bar{x})^2, \] and only the first term depends on \(\mu\). Hence \[ p(x_1, \ldots, x_N | \mu) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{N(\mu - \bar{x})^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \] which is the likelihood of a single observation \(\bar{x}\) with variance \(\sigma^2/N\).

We can therefore reuse the single-observation results, with \(x\) replaced by \(\bar{x}\) and \(\sigma^2\) by \(\sigma^2/N\). The posterior parameters become \[\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{\tau_N^2} &= \frac{1}{\tau_0^2} + \frac{N}{\sigma^2}, \\ \mu_N &= \frac{\frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} + \frac{N\bar{x}}{\sigma^2}}{\frac{1}{\tau_0^2} + \frac{N}{\sigma^2}}. \end{aligned}\]Each observation adds information, and the posterior precision grows with the amount of data. For \(N = 1\) these equations reduce to the single-observation results.

This one-dimensional example shows the logic of Bayesian updating. We combine sources of information according to their precision. The same principle applies to the multivariate case that linear regression needs.

5.4 Multivariate Gaussian Conjugacy

We now extend this pattern to many dimensions, as linear regression requires. The step from one dimension to many may seem hard, but the principles stay the same.

A one-dimensional Gaussian is set by its mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and a multivariate Gaussian by its mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). The diagonal of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) holds the uncertainty of each parameter. The off-diagonal terms show how the parameters vary together. This matters in linear regression, because slope and intercept estimates are often correlated.

The multivariate Gaussian density generalizes the one-dimensional form \[ \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2}\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right), \] where \(D\) is the dimension of \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) is the determinant of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). The quadratic form \((\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\) generalizes the squared distance \((x-\mu)^2/\sigma^2\) of one dimension, and it includes the correlations between the dimensions.

The main result of one dimension carries over to many dimensions. The product of two Gaussians is, up to a constant, again a Gaussian. This is what makes Bayesian linear regression analytically tractable.

Consider two multivariate Gaussian distributions \[\begin{aligned} p_1(\mathbf{x}) &= \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1), \\ p_2(\mathbf{x}) &= \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_2,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2). \end{aligned}\]

As in one dimension, we multiply the distributions and keep only the exponential terms \[ p_1(\mathbf{x})p_2(\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left[(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1) + (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\right]\right). \]

To show that the product is Gaussian, we must bring the combined exponent into the standard quadratic form. We expand both quadratic terms \[\begin{aligned} &-\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 \right. \nonumber \\ &\quad\quad \left. + \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2 + \boldsymbol{\mu}_2^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2\right]. \end{aligned}\]

The covariance matrices are symmetric, so the cross terms \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_i^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i^{-1}\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_i\) are equal scalars. Collecting terms by powers of \(\mathbf{x}\) gives \[\begin{aligned} &-\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathbf{x}^T(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1})\mathbf{x} - 2(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_2^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1})\mathbf{x} + \text{const}\right]. \end{aligned}\]This has the quadratic form of a multivariate Gaussian. Comparing it with the standard form lets us identify the parameters of the result. If the result is \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\rm prod},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\rm prod})\), then the quadratic and linear terms give \[\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\rm prod}^{-1} &= \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1}, \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\rm prod}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\rm prod} &= \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2. \end{aligned}\]

Solving for the parameters of the product gives \[\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\rm prod} &= (\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1} + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1})^{-1}, \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\rm prod} &= \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\rm prod}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_2^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_2). \end{aligned}\]These expressions generalize the one-dimensional results. The precision matrix (inverse covariance) of the product is the sum of the input precision matrices. The mean of the product is a precision-weighted average of the input means. The matrix algebra looks more complex, but the pattern is the same, because we combine information weighted by its precision. Figure 5.4 shows two Gaussians and their product.

The Gaussian product rule matters for linear regression. A Gaussian prior on the parameters and a Gaussian likelihood give a Gaussian posterior. We then have analytical expressions for the updated estimates and their uncertainties.

The same approach covers one parameter or dozens of regression coefficients. In each case we combine prior knowledge and observational evidence, weighted by precision. We use this again in the more complex models of later chapters.

5.5 Mathematics of Bayesian Linear Regression

We can now derive the full Bayesian solution for linear regression. Our goal is the posterior distribution \(p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{S})\) of the parameters. We condition on the observed data \(\mathbf{t}\), the input features \(\mathbf{X}\) and the measurement variances, which we collect in the diagonal matrix \(\mathbf{S}\). Together they form the data \(\mathcal{D}\). The posterior gives our best estimates of the regression coefficients, our confidence in them, and how they correlate. Figure 5.5 compares the Bayesian result with the maximum likelihood fit.

We start again from Bayes’ theorem \[ p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{S}) \propto p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{X},\mathbf{w},\mathbf{S})p(\mathbf{w}). \]

Chapter 4 showed that, for Gaussian measurement uncertainties, the likelihood is \[ p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{X},\mathbf{w},\mathbf{S}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{t}|\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w},\mathbf{S}), \] where \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) is the design matrix. It holds the basis functions \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) evaluated at each input point, with one row for each point and one column for each feature. For a polynomial of degree 2 and two input points \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), it is \[ \boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x_1 & x_1^2 \\ 1 & x_2 & x_2^2 \end{bmatrix}. \]For a straight-line fit of the M-\(\sigma\) relation, row \(i\) is \((1, \log\sigma_{\star,i})\).

For the prior, we choose a multivariate Gaussian distribution, the natural conjugate prior for our Gaussian likelihood \[ p(\mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{m}_0,\mathbf{S}_0). \] Here \(\mathbf{m}_0\) is our prior belief about the most likely parameter values, and \(\mathbf{S}_0\) holds our prior uncertainties and correlations between the parameters. A common choice is \(\mathbf{S}_0 = \eta^2\mathrm{Id}\), where \(\eta\) is the prior standard deviation of each weight and \(\mathrm{Id}\) is the identity matrix. We call such a prior isotropic. It gives the weights the same variance and no correlation with one another.

The choice of prior needs care in astronomy. For the M-\(\sigma\) relation, we could set \(\mathbf{m}_0\) from earlier studies, for example a slope near 4 and an intercept that agrees with theoretical predictions. Then \(\mathbf{S}_0\) would hold our uncertainty in them. The off-diagonal term of \(\mathbf{S}_0\) would hold the expected correlation between the slope and the intercept.

Rewriting the Likelihood

To use the multivariate conjugacy result, we need the likelihood and the prior as Gaussians in the parameter vector \(\mathbf{w}\). The prior already has this form. The likelihood is a Gaussian in the observations \(\mathbf{t}\), so we must rewrite it as a Gaussian in \(\mathbf{w}\).

We start with the likelihood and write out its quadratic form \[ p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{t}|\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w},\mathbf{S}) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{t}-\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w})^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}(\mathbf{t}-\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w})\right). \]Expanding the quadratic form gives \[ (\mathbf{t}-\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w})^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}(\mathbf{t}-\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t} - 2\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}. \]The first term does not depend on \(\mathbf{w}\), so we absorb it into the proportionality. The terms that depend on \(\mathbf{w}\) give \[ p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{w}) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{w}^T(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi})\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{w}^T(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t})\right). \]

Comparing this with the standard Gaussian form in \(\mathbf{w}\), we can write it as \[ p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{w}) \propto \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1), \] where \[\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1} &= \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}, \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 &= \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t}. \end{aligned}\]Solving for the likelihood parameters gives \[\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1 &= (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}, \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 &= (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t}. \end{aligned}\]Notice that \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\) is the maximum likelihood estimate that we derived in Chapter 4. The likelihood, viewed as a function of the parameters, has the shape of a Gaussian centered on that estimate.

The Posterior of the Weights

Now we apply the multivariate conjugacy result. The posterior after \(N\) data points is the product of two Gaussians \[ p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t}) \propto \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{m}_0,\mathbf{S}_0) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{m}_N,\mathbf{S}_N), \] where, by the conjugacy formulas, \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_N^{-1} &= \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1} + \mathbf{S}_0^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi} + \mathbf{S}_0^{-1}, \\ \mathbf{m}_N &= \mathbf{S}_N(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_1^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \mathbf{S}_0^{-1}\mathbf{m}_0) = \mathbf{S}_N(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t} + \mathbf{S}_0^{-1}\mathbf{m}_0). \end{aligned}\]The complete Bayesian linear regression solution is therefore \[ p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{S}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{m}_N,\mathbf{S}_N), \] where \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_N &= (\mathbf{S}_0^{-1} + \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}, \\ \mathbf{m}_N &= \mathbf{S}_N(\mathbf{S}_0^{-1}\mathbf{m}_0 + \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t}). \end{aligned}\]These expressions generalize our one-dimensional results. The posterior precision \(\mathbf{S}_N^{-1}\) is the sum of the prior precision \(\mathbf{S}_0^{-1}\) and the data precision \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\). The posterior mean \(\mathbf{m}_N\) is a precision-weighted combination of our prior belief \(\mathbf{m}_0\) and the data term \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t}\), which contains the maximum likelihood estimate.

A draw from \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{m}_N,\mathbf{S}_N)\) is one plausible parameter vector, and so one plausible line. The thin lines in Figure 5.5(b) are such draws. The shaded band is the 95% credible interval of the line. Section 5.7 explains how we compute it.

Limiting Cases

Limiting cases build intuition about this general solution. The first has minimal prior knowledge. We take the isotropic prior \(\mathbf{S}_0 = \eta^2\mathrm{Id}\) with \(\eta^2 \to \infty\), and \(\mathbf{m}_0 = \mathbf{0}\). In this uninformative limit we get \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_N &\to (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}, \\ \mathbf{m}_N &\to (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t}. \end{aligned}\]The posterior mean reduces to the maximum likelihood estimate, so the Bayesian and frequentist point estimates agree when prior knowledge is minimal. On top of the point estimate, we obtain the covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}_N\), which describes our uncertainty about the parameters given the data.

In a simple special case, with homogeneous measurement uncertainties, \(\mathbf{S} = \sigma^2\mathrm{Id}\), and an isotropic prior, \(\mathbf{S}_0 = \eta^2\mathrm{Id}\) with \(\mathbf{m}_0 = \mathbf{0}\), the expressions simplify to \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{S}_N &= \left(\frac{1}{\eta^2}\mathrm{Id} + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi}\right)^{-1}, \\ \mathbf{m}_N &= \left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\eta^2}\mathrm{Id} + \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi}\right)^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t}. \end{aligned}\]Compare this with the ordinary least squares solution \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}} = (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t}\) of Chapter 4. The Bayesian solution has an extra regularization term \((\sigma^2/\eta^2)\mathrm{Id}\), which discourages large weights (Section 5.6). This ratio of measurement variance to prior variance sets the tradeoff between fitting the data and our prior beliefs.

A second limiting case is a large number of observations. As \(N\) grows, the data term \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) typically grows in proportion to \(N\), so \(\mathbf{S}_N\) shrinks roughly as \(1/N\). Parameter uncertainty therefore decreases as we collect more data. The standard deviation of each parameter falls roughly as \(1/\sqrt{N}\), as for the sample mean in Chapter 3. For \(N \to \infty\), the posterior concentrates around the true parameter values if the linear model describes the data.

The Bayesian solution is analytical. Unlike many advanced methods, it needs no iterative numerical optimization. It gives the parameter uncertainties with little computation. Astronomical applications often need such uncertainties for scientific inference. The off-diagonal terms of \(\mathbf{S}_N\) matter in practice.

Correlation Between Slope and Intercept

Consider a mass-luminosity relation for stars, \(L = A M^\gamma\). In logarithmic form, \(\log L = \gamma \log M + \log A\). The power-law index \(\gamma\) tells us how luminosity scales with mass, and the normalization \(A\) sets the overall luminosity scale. The posterior covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}_N\) typically shows that these parameters are correlated. For mostly positive inputs, a lower normalization can compensate for a slightly steeper slope and fit the same data. We must understand these degeneracies when we use such relations to make predictions or to compare with theoretical models.

The size of this correlation depends on where we place the intercept. It is strong when the intercept, the value of the line at \(x = 0\), lies far outside the data, as in the M-\(\sigma\) relation. We can remove it by writing the model as \(y = w_0 + w_1(x - x_{\rm p})\), so that \(w_0\) is the value of the line at a pivot \(x_{\rm p}\). The data precision matrix then reads \[ \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} \Omega & \sum_i \omega_i (x_i - x_{\rm p}) \\ \sum_i \omega_i (x_i - x_{\rm p}) & \sum_i \omega_i (x_i - x_{\rm p})^2 \end{bmatrix}, \] where \(\omega_i = 1/\sigma_i^2\) and \(\Omega = \sum_i \omega_i\).

The off-diagonal entry vanishes when \(x_{\rm p}\) is the inverse-variance weighted mean of the inputs, \(x_{\rm p} = \sum_i \omega_i x_i / \Omega\). The matrix is then diagonal, and so is its inverse \(\mathbf{S}_N\) in the uninformative limit. The parameters \(w_0\) and \(w_1\) are therefore uncorrelated, and \(w_0\) has variance \(1/\Omega\). This is the smallest variance of \(w_0\) for any choice of \(x_{\rm p}\), because the data constrain the line best at their weighted mean. Astronomers use this idea when they write the M-\(\sigma\) relation with \(\log(\sigma_\star/200\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}})\).

5.6 Prior as Regularization

The examples above have only a few parameters. Many problems in astronomy and machine learning have far more, so they need regularization, a penalty on large parameter values that guards against overfitting.

For a stellar spectrum, we might use hundreds or thousands of spectral features as basis functions to estimate the temperature, surface gravity and chemical abundances. Examples are absorption line strengths and continuum measurements. The number of weights can approach the number of data points, so such a model overfits easily. A high-degree polynomial does the same, because it can fit a few data points exactly and oscillate between them. Regularization helps in such cases. It finds solutions that generalize better, because it stops the model from over-weighting any single spectral feature.

MAP Estimation and Ridge Regression

We now link maximizing the posterior probability to minimizing a regularized loss function. Instead of the full posterior distribution, we look for the single most probable parameter values, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate \[ \mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t},\mathbf{X},\sigma^2). \]

Here \(\arg\max_{\mathbf{w}}\) means the value of \(\mathbf{w}\) at which the expression after it is largest. The logarithm is a monotonic function, so maximizing the log-posterior is equivalent to maximizing the posterior itself. Bayes’ theorem gives \[ \ln p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t},\mathbf{X},\sigma^2) = \ln p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{X},\sigma^2) + \ln p(\mathbf{w}) + \text{const}. \]

We take homogeneous noise, \(\mathbf{S} = \sigma^2\mathrm{Id}\), and a zero-mean isotropic prior, \(p(\mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{0},\eta^2\mathrm{Id})\). We then evaluate each term explicitly.

The likelihood term measures the fit of the model predictions to the data \[\begin{aligned} \ln p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{w},\mathbf{X},\sigma^2) &= \ln \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{t}|\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w},\sigma^2\mathrm{Id}) \\ &= -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w})^T(\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}) + \text{const} \\ &= -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}\|^2 + \text{const}. \end{aligned}\]This is the negative of the sum of squared residuals that we minimized in maximum likelihood estimation, scaled by \(1/(2\sigma^2)\). Here \(\|\mathbf{v}\|\), the L2 norm, is the Euclidean length of a vector \(\mathbf{v}\), so \(\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{v}\).

The prior term describes our belief about the parameter values \[\begin{aligned} \ln p(\mathbf{w}) &= \ln \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{0},\eta^2\mathrm{Id}) \\ &= -\frac{1}{2\eta^2}\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{w} + \text{const} \\ &= -\frac{1}{2\eta^2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + \text{const}. \end{aligned}\]

A zero-mean prior expresses a specific belief. Before we see the data, we expect each coefficient to be near zero. This follows Occam’s razor, the principle that among competing explanations we prefer the one with the fewest assumptions.

A large coefficient means that the model leans heavily on one feature, and a coefficient near zero means a weak dependence. When several models fit the data equally well, the prior favors the one without unnecessary dependence on single features, unless the evidence demands it. This assumption suits problems with many features that each have a small effect, such as spectra with thousands of pixels. Shrinking the coefficients adds some bias, a systematic offset of the estimates from the true values. It also lowers their variance, the scatter of the estimates from one data set to another. This exchange is the bias-variance tradeoff of Section 4.7.

If we expect large coefficients for physical reasons, we use a wider prior or a nonzero mean. If we expect only a few important features, we use a prior that favors exact zeros.

We combine the two terms and define \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\eta^2\) \[\begin{aligned} \ln p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t},\mathbf{X},\sigma^2) &= -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}\|^2 - \frac{1}{2\eta^2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + \text{const} \\ &= -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left[\|\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}\|^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2\right] + \text{const}. \end{aligned}\]Maximizing this log-posterior is equivalent to minimizing the regularized loss function \[ E(\mathbf{w}) = \|\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}\|^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2. \]This result links Bayesian inference and regularization. The first term, \(\|\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}\|^2\), measures how well the model predictions match the observations. The second term, \(\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2\), is L2 regularization, also called ridge regression or Tikhonov regularization. It implements the Occam’s razor preference for solutions that depend weakly on the features. It penalizes large coefficients unless they give a much better fit to the data.

The posterior is Gaussian, so its peak, the MAP estimate, coincides with its mean. The minimizer of \(E(\mathbf{w})\) is the posterior mean \(\mathbf{m}_N\) of the last section, so the term \((\sigma^2/\eta^2)\mathrm{Id}\) found there is the ridge penalty. Machine learning uses the same penalty widely, called weight decay in neural networks, and the prior gives it a statistical basis (Chapter 15).

The regularization parameter \(\lambda = \sigma^2/\eta^2\) is the ratio of the measurement variance to the prior variance. When \(\lambda\) is large (noisy measurements or a confident prior), the regularization term dominates. It forces the solution toward simpler models with smaller parameter values. When \(\lambda\) is small (precise measurements or an uncertain prior), the data term dominates. The model can then follow the observations more closely with more complex fits. Figure 5.6 shows the effect of \(\lambda\).

We can choose \(\lambda\) by cross-validation (Section 4.7), which scores each trial value on data held out of the fit. The prior width \(\eta\) is a hyperparameter of the Bayesian model too, and we still set it on validation data. The Bayesian view ties \(\lambda\) to the ratio \(\sigma^2/\eta^2\), so we can also set it from the measurement uncertainties and the plausible parameter ranges. This helps in astronomy, where physical constraints often give strong guidance on plausible parameters. We can also choose \(\lambda\) by maximizing the evidence \(p(\mathcal{D})\), as Chapter 14 does for Gaussian processes.

Laplace Prior

Different priors lead to different regularization schemes. A Laplace prior centered at zero, with scale \(\kappa\), has the probability density \(p(w_j) = \exp(-|w_j|/\kappa)/(2\kappa)\) for each weight. For independent weights, \(p(\mathbf{w}) \propto \exp(-\|\mathbf{w}\|_1/\kappa)\), where \(\|\mathbf{w}\|_1 = \sum_j |w_j|\) is the L1 norm. Minimizing the negative log-posterior then gives L1 regularization, also called the lasso, with the loss function \[ E(\mathbf{w}) = \|\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}\|^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|_1, \] where \(\lambda = 2\sigma^2/\kappa\).

The Laplace prior peaks sharply at zero, whereas a Gaussian prior is smooth there. The L1 penalty has a kink at zero, so the MAP estimate can set some coefficients exactly to zero. A solution with many zero coefficients is called sparse. This fits problems in which only a few features matter. Only the MAP estimate is sparse. The full posterior of a Laplace prior is not sparse and has no simple closed form.

Several common regularizers have a Bayesian reading, with a Gaussian prior for ridge regression and a Laplace prior for the lasso. The Bayesian view guides the choice of regularization from domain knowledge and the structure we expect in good solutions. Sparsity constraints in image reconstruction and smoothness penalties in function approximation also correspond to suitable priors.

The MAP estimate is a regularized point solution. The full posterior holds more information.

This difference matters in astronomy. For the M-\(\sigma\) relation, the MAP estimate gives a best-fit slope and intercept. The full posterior also tells us how uncertain these parameters are and how they correlate.

5.7 Posterior Predictive Distribution

So far we have found the distribution of the model parameters. In many applications the goal is to predict new observations. An astronomer who measures the velocity dispersion of a galaxy and wants its black hole mass from the M-\(\sigma\) relation needs more than parameter estimates. They need the full uncertainty of the prediction.

The posterior predictive distribution provides this. It puts measurement noise and parameter uncertainty into one prediction. Rather than a point prediction, it gives a complete probability distribution.

For a new input \(\mathbf{x}_*\) with output \(y_*\), we define the posterior predictive distribution as \[ p(y_* | \mathbf{x}_*, \mathcal{D}) = \int p(y_* | \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{w}) p(\mathbf{w} | \mathcal{D})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{w}. \]This integral has a simple meaning. For each parameter set \(\mathbf{w}\) consistent with our data, we predict the distribution of \(y_*\). We then average over all sets, weighted by their probabilities given the data. The prediction thus includes our parameter uncertainty.

A Gaussian likelihood, a Gaussian posterior and a linear model allow us to evaluate this integral analytically. Both factors under the integral are Gaussian. The predictive likelihood is \(p(y_* | \mathbf{x}_*, \mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{N}(y_* | \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{w}, \sigma^2)\). Here \(\sigma^2\) is the measurement variance of the new observation. The posterior is \(p(\mathbf{w} | \mathcal{D}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{w} | \mathbf{m}_N, \mathbf{S}_N)\).

By the product rule of Section 2.5, the product of the two factors is the joint distribution of \(y_*\) and \(\mathbf{w}\). It is Gaussian, because \(y_*\) is a linear function of \(\mathbf{w}\) plus Gaussian noise. When we marginalize a joint Gaussian distribution, that is, integrate out some of its variables, the result is again Gaussian. The posterior predictive distribution is therefore Gaussian, so we only need its mean and variance. The first appendix of this chapter proves this property.

We find the mean and variance with two tools from Chapter 3. The law of total expectation is \(\mathbb{E}[y_*] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}}[\mathbb{E}[y_*|\mathbf{w}]]\). For a fixed parameter vector \(\mathbf{w}\), our model predicts \(y_* = \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{w}\) plus zero-mean noise. Taking the expectation over the posterior gives \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[y_*] &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}}[\mathbb{E}[y_*|\mathbf{w}]] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}}[\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{w}] \\ &= \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}}[\mathbf{w}] \\ &= \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{m}_N. \end{aligned}\]This result agrees with intuition. Our best prediction at \(\mathbf{x}_*\) uses our best parameter estimate \(\mathbf{m}_N\) with the basis functions \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)\).

The law of total variance, \(\text{Var}[y_*] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}}[\text{Var}[y_*|\mathbf{w}]] + \text{Var}_{\mathbf{w}}[\mathbb{E}[y_*|\mathbf{w}]]\), shows two sources of uncertainty in our predictions. The first term is the aleatoric uncertainty, the randomness of the measurements. Even if we knew the model parameters exactly, repeated observations would scatter because of instrumental noise, photon statistics and other random effects. For our model this term is \[ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}}[\text{Var}[y_*|\mathbf{w}]] = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}}[\sigma^2] = \sigma^2. \]More data cannot reduce this part, because each new observation still scatters by \(\sigma\). Averaging many observations only shrinks the uncertainty of their mean.

The second term is the epistemic uncertainty, our imperfect knowledge of the true model parameters. It arises because the data are finite and noisy. We evaluate it as follows \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}_{\mathbf{w}}[\mathbb{E}[y_*|\mathbf{w}]] &= \text{Var}_{\mathbf{w}}[\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{w}] \\ &= \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\text{Var}_{\mathbf{w}}[\mathbf{w}]\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*) \\ &= \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{S}_N\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*). \end{aligned}\]This is the variance of the line at \(\mathbf{x}_*\). Unlike the aleatoric part, this component shrinks as we collect more training data, because more observations constrain the parameters.

Combining the two contributions gives the posterior predictive distribution \[ p(y_* | \mathbf{x}_*, \mathcal{D}) = \mathcal{N}(y_* | \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T \mathbf{m}_N, \sigma^2 + \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T \mathbf{S}_N \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)). \]This expression includes both sources of predictive uncertainty. The mean \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T \mathbf{m}_N\) is our best estimate. The variance \(\sigma^2 + \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T \mathbf{S}_N \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)\) is the sum of the measurement noise and the parameter uncertainty.

The two terms give two different intervals, and Figure 5.7 shows both. The line value \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{w}\) is a linear function of the Gaussian \(\mathbf{w}\), so it is Gaussian with mean \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{m}_N\) and variance \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{S}_N\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)\). A new observation \(y_*\) adds the noise \(\sigma^2\). A Gaussian has 95% of its probability within 1.96 standard deviations of its mean, so the 95% intervals are \[\begin{aligned} \text{line:} &\quad \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{m}_N \pm 1.96\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{S}_N\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)}, \\ \text{new observation:} &\quad \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{m}_N \pm 1.96\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T\mathbf{S}_N\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)}. \end{aligned}\]

The first interval is the shaded band in Figures 5.5 to 5.7. It describes the line alone. The second interval, the predictive interval for a new observation, is wider because it also includes the noise \(\sigma^2\). The sideways curves in Figure 5.7 show the full predictive distribution behind it.

The decomposition shows how the uncertainty varies with the input. The parameter uncertainty term \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T \mathbf{S}_N \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)\) typically grows as we move away from the training data. Extrapolation beyond the observed range therefore carries a larger uncertainty than interpolation within it. For the M-\(\sigma\) relation, we should be more cautious about black hole mass predictions for galaxies with velocity dispersions far from our training sample.

The quadratic form \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)^T \mathbf{S}_N \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_*)\) depends on the features at the prediction point and on the parameter covariance. Regions of feature space that the training data constrain poorly have a higher predictive uncertainty. This shows where new observations help most.

To carry this uncertainty into a larger analysis, we can draw samples from the predictive distribution instead of using a point prediction. This matters in astronomical pipelines, where uncertainties must be tracked through several processing stages.

So far we have assumed that the inputs \(\mathbf{x}\) are exact and that only the outputs carry measurement errors. In astronomy, both often carry errors. Ignoring the errors in the inputs flattens the fitted slope. Chapter 6 corrects this.

5.8 Appendix: Marginal Distribution of a Multivariate Gaussian

We asserted that the posterior predictive distribution is Gaussian. The integrand is a joint Gaussian in \(y_*\) and \(\mathbf{w}\), and integrating out \(\mathbf{w}\) leaves a marginal Gaussian in \(y_*\). This follows from a general theorem. Integrating out some variables of a joint multivariate Gaussian leaves a Gaussian.

This result underlies many calculations in Bayesian inference, so we prove it. We show that for a joint multivariate Gaussian over partitioned variables, the marginal distribution of any subset is Gaussian.

Statement of the Result

Consider a joint multivariate Gaussian distribution over partitioned variables \[ \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}_1 \\ \mathbf{x}_2 \end{bmatrix} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left( \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}_1\\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_2 \end{bmatrix},\; \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22} \end{bmatrix} \right), \] where \(\mathbf{x}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{D_1}\) and \(\mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{D_2}\) are vectors of \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) real numbers. We partition the covariance matrix accordingly.

We prove that the marginal distribution of \(\mathbf{x}_1\) is \[ \mathbf{x}_1 \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}\right). \]

Proof

The joint probability density function is \[ p(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{(D_1+D_2)/2}\sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_1\\ \mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2\end{bmatrix}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_1\\ \mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2\end{bmatrix}\right). \]

To find the marginal distribution \(p(\mathbf{x}_1)\), we integrate over \(\mathbf{x}_2\) \[ p(\mathbf{x}_1) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{D_2}} p(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_2. \]

We define \(\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{x}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_1\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2\) for simplicity. We partition the precision matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) as \[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11} & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\\ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21} & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22} \end{bmatrix}, \] where the dimensions match the partitioning of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\).

The quadratic form in the exponent becomes \[ \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{u}\\ \mathbf{v}\end{bmatrix}^T\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11} & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\\ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21} & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{u}\\ \mathbf{v}\end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{u}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{u}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{v}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}\mathbf{v}. \]

The matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) is symmetric, as the inverse of a symmetric matrix. Hence \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}^T\), and \[ \mathbf{u}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{v}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}\mathbf{u} = 2\mathbf{v}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}\mathbf{u}. \]

The integral becomes \[ p(\mathbf{x}_1) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{(D_1+D_2)/2}\sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}\mathbf{u}\right) \int_{\mathbb{R}^{D_2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}[\mathbf{v}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}\mathbf{v} + 2\mathbf{v}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}\mathbf{u}]\right)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v}. \]

To evaluate the integral, we complete the square in \(\mathbf{v}\). We define \(\mathbf{b} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}\mathbf{u}\), so the quadratic form in \(\mathbf{v}\) is \[ \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{v}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{b})^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}(\mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{b}) - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{b}. \]The integral over the completed square is a standard Gaussian integral \[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{D_2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{b})^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}(\mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{b})\right)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v} = (2\pi)^{D_2/2}[\det(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22})]^{-1/2}. \]

Combining the results gives \[\begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{x}_1) &= \frac{(2\pi)^{D_2/2}}{(2\pi)^{(D_1+D_2)/2}\sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22})}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}\mathbf{u} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{b}\right) \\ &= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D_1/2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}\sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22})}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}^T[\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}]\mathbf{u}\right). \end{aligned}\]The exponent contains the matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}\), the Schur complement of \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}\). For a block matrix, the upper left block of the inverse is the inverse of the Schur complement of the lower right block. Here the block matrix is \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) and its inverse is \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), so \[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} = (\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11} - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21})^{-1}. \]

The Schur complement also gives a determinant relation. The determinant of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\) is \(\det\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}\) times the determinant of the Schur complement. Both block matrix results follow by factoring the block matrix into block triangular pieces. By the previous equation, the Schur complement has determinant \(1/\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}\), and hence \[ \sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}\sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22})} = \sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11})}. \]Substituting these relationships gives \[ p(\mathbf{x}_1) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D_1/2}\sqrt{\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11})}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}_1-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_1-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1)\right). \]This is the probability density function of \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_1|\boldsymbol{\mu}_1,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11})\), which completes the proof.

This result matters for Bayesian calculations. When we integrate over the parameter uncertainty to obtain predictions, the result keeps the Gaussian form with analytically computable parameters. We can also compute the marginal likelihood (evidence) analytically by integrating over the parameter priors, which allows model comparison (Chapter 14).

Together with conjugacy, the Gaussian form under marginalization makes tractable many Bayesian calculations that would otherwise need numerical integration.

5.9 Appendix: Conditional Distribution of a Multivariate Gaussian

Chapters 13 and 14 use the conditional distribution of one part of a joint Gaussian given the other part. We derive it here for the joint Gaussian of Section 5.8.

Statement of the Result

Consider again the joint multivariate Gaussian distribution over partitioned variables \[ \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}_1 \\ \mathbf{x}_2 \end{bmatrix} \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\!\left( \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\mu}_1\\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_2 \end{bmatrix},\; \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21} & \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22} \end{bmatrix} \right). \] We prove that the conditional distribution of \(\mathbf{x}_1\) given \(\mathbf{x}_2\) is \[ p(\mathbf{x}_1|\mathbf{x}_2) = \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{x}_1\,\Big|\,\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2),\; \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}\right). \] The mean is a linear function of \(\mathbf{x}_2\), and the covariance does not depend on \(\mathbf{x}_2\).

Proof

As in Section 5.8, we define \(\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{x}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_1\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2\). We write \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{ij}\) for the blocks of the precision matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\), which is symmetric, so \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12} = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}^T\). The joint density is proportional to the exponential of \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\) times the quadratic form \[ \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{u}\\ \mathbf{v}\end{bmatrix}^T\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11} & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\\ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21} & \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{u}\\ \mathbf{v}\end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{u}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}\mathbf{u} + 2\mathbf{u}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{v}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}\mathbf{v}. \]

We keep \(\mathbf{x}_2\) fixed and look at the density as a function of \(\mathbf{x}_1\). The term with \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{22}\) does not contain \(\mathbf{u}\), so only the first two terms matter. We complete the square in \(\mathbf{u}\) \[ \mathbf{u}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}\mathbf{u} + 2\mathbf{u}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\mathbf{v} = (\mathbf{u} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\mathbf{v})^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}(\mathbf{u} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\mathbf{v}) - \mathbf{v}^T\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{21}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\mathbf{v}. \] The last term does not depend on \(\mathbf{x}_1\). The density of \(\mathbf{x}_1\) is therefore a Gaussian with covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}^{-1}\) and mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}(\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\).

We now write both in terms of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). The relation \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathrm{Id}\) gives \[\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22} &= \mathbf{0}, \\ \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21} &= \mathrm{Id}. \end{aligned}\] The first relation gives \(-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{12} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\), and the second then gives \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{11}^{-1} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{11} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{12}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{22}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{21}\). Substituting both into the mean and the covariance gives the stated result, which completes the proof.

5.10 Tutorial: Stellar Temperature Uncertainties

This tutorial applies the posterior and the predictive distribution of this chapter to stellar temperatures predicted from spectra. Errors in these temperatures propagate into stellar ages and abundances. Each prediction therefore needs an uncertainty. The full tutorial can be found at https://tingyuansen.github.io/statml/ as tutorial 5.

The tutorial returns to the APOGEE spectra of Section 4.8. A regularized fit predicts each temperature (Figure 5.8a), but it does not say how far to trust it. The tutorial adds simulated noise of known size to the pipeline temperatures and treats the result as the measured temperatures.

The regularized fit gives the peak of the posterior of the weights for a Gaussian prior (Section 5.6). The Bayesian treatment keeps the whole posterior, which has a closed form (Section 5.5). Different weights that the data allow give different predictions for a new star, and their spread is the uncertainty. The posterior predictive distribution of Section 5.7 adds the noise of the new star. The tutorial adds a scatter for the misfit of the linear model. Each star then has a 95 percent interval of its own (Figure 5.8b).

We can check these intervals on the test stars, after the validation stars set the prior width. An interval is honest when it contains the measured temperature as often as it claims, as the intervals of Figure 5.8b do. Honest intervals let us carry the temperature errors into stellar ages and abundances. The prior keeps the fit from overfitting, and the posterior predictive distribution turns each prediction into such an interval.

Further Reading

Laplace (1820) treated inverse probability, an early form of Bayesian inference. Zellner (1971) applies Bayesian methods to regression problems in econometrics. Lindley (1965) covers probability and statistics from a Bayesian viewpoint. Raiffa and Schlaifer (1961) developed conjugate priors, which make Bayesian regression analytically tractable, and DeGroot (1970) treats their properties. Anderson (1958) develops the multivariate Gaussian theory that underlies Bayesian linear regression. Tikhonov (1963) developed regularization methods, and Hoerl and Kennard (1970) developed ridge regression. Tibshirani (1996) introduced the lasso, the sparse MAP estimate under a Laplace prior. MacKay (1992) showed how to set regularization parameters with the Bayesian evidence, which links machine learning and Bayesian inference. Kass and Raftery (1995) review Bayes factors and ways to compute the marginal likelihood for model comparison.
